# xmlparser - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/xmlparser/

## Expand description

*xmlparser* is a low-level, pull-based, zero-allocation
[XML 1.0](https://www.w3.org/TR/xml/) parser.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
for token in xmlparser::Tokenizer::from("<tagname name='value'/>") {
    println!("{:?}", token);
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#why-a-new-library)Why a new library?

This library is basically a low-level XML tokenizer that preserves the positions of the tokens
and is not intended to be used directly.
If you are looking for a higher level solution, check out
[roxmltree](https://github.com/RazrFalcon/roxmltree).

[§](https://docs.rs#benefits)Benefits

- All tokens contain `StrSpan`structs which represent the position of the substring in the original document.
- Good error processing. All error types contain the position (line:column) where it occurred.
- No heap allocations.
- No dependencies.
- Tiny. ~1400 LOC and ~30KiB in the release build according to `cargo-bloat`.
- Supports `no_std`builds. To use without the standard library, disable the default features.

[§](https://docs.rs#limitations)Limitations

- Currently, only ENTITY objects are parsed from the DOCTYPE. All others are ignored.
- No tree structure validation. So an XML like `<root><child></root></child>`or a string without root element will be parsed without errors. You should check for this manually. On the other hand`<a/><a/>`will lead to an error.
- Duplicated attributes is not an error. So XML like `<item a="v1" a="v2"/>`will be parsed without errors. You should check for this manually.
- UTF-8 only.

[§](https://docs.rs#safety)Safety

- The library must not panic. Any panic is considered a critical bug and should be reported.
- The library forbids unsafe code.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [StrSpan](https://docs.rs/struct.StrSpan.html)
- A string slice.
- [Stream](https://docs.rs/struct.Stream.html)
- A streaming XML parsing interface.
- [TextPos](https://docs.rs/struct.TextPos.html)
- Position in text.
- [Tokenizer](https://docs.rs/struct.Tokenizer.html)
- Tokenizer for the XML structure.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Element](https://docs.rs/enum.ElementEnd.html)- End
- `ElementEnd`token.
- [Entity](https://docs.rs/enum.EntityDefinition.html)- Definition
- Representation of the [EntityDef](https://www.w3.org/TR/xml/#NT-EntityDef)value.
- [Error](https://docs.rs/enum.Error.html)
- An XML parser errors.
- [External](https://docs.rs/enum.ExternalId.html)- Id
- Representation of the [ExternalID](https://www.w3.org/TR/xml/#NT-ExternalID)value.
- [Reference](https://docs.rs/enum.Reference.html)
- Representation of the [Reference](https://www.w3.org/TR/xml/#NT-Reference)value.
- [Stream](https://docs.rs/enum.StreamError.html)- Error
- A stream parser errors.
- [Token](https://docs.rs/enum.Token.html)
- An XML token.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [XmlByte](https://docs.rs/trait.XmlByteExt.html)- Ext
- Extension methods for XML-subset only operations.
- [XmlChar](https://docs.rs/trait.XmlCharExt.html)- Ext
- Extension methods for XML-subset only operations.

# xmlparser 0.13.6 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/xmlparser/latest

## xmlparser

*xmlparser* is a low-level, pull-based, zero-allocation
[XML 1.0](https://www.w3.org/TR/xml/) parser.

### Example

```
for token in from
```
### Why a new library?

This library is basically a low-level XML tokenizer that preserves the positions of the tokens
and is not intended to be used directly.
If you are looking for a higher level solution, check out
[roxmltree](https://github.com/RazrFalcon/roxmltree).

### Benefits

- All tokens contain `StrSpan`structs which represent the position of the substring in the original document.
- Good error processing. All error types contain the position (line:column) where it occurred.
- No heap allocations.
- No dependencies.
- Tiny. ~1400 LOC and ~30KiB in the release build according to `cargo-bloat`.
- Supports `no_std`builds. To use without the standard library, disable the default features.

### Limitations

- Currently, only ENTITY objects are parsed from the DOCTYPE. All others are ignored.
- No tree structure validation. So an XML like `<root><child></root></child>`or a string without root element will be parsed without errors. You should check for this manually. On the other hand`<a/><a/>`will lead to an error.
- Duplicated attributes is not an error. So XML like `<item a="v1" a="v2"/>`will be parsed without errors. You should check for this manually.
- UTF-8 only.

### Safety

- The library must not panic. Any panic is considered a critical bug and should be reported.
- The library forbids unsafe code.

# About Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/about

Docs.rs is an
            [open source](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs)
            documentation host for crates of the
            [Rust Programming Language](https://www.rust-lang.org/).
            All libraries published to [crates.io](https://crates.io)
            are documented. If you just published a crate, your crate is likely
            still in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

            The source code of Docs.rs is available on
            [GitHub](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs). If
            you ever encounter an issue, don't hesitate to report it! (And
            thanks in advance!)

Currently running Docs.rs version is: **0.0.0 (964c90a45859fd8f9076e3cbe58470a5a4f4d4f7 2026-07-01 )**

Summaries of the documentation build processes [are available at /releases/](https://docs.rs/releases).

            JavaScript in support of documentation is allowed but not guaranteed to work on docs.rs. What that
            means: If you write documentation that inlines some JavaScript (like
            [KaTeX](https://katex.org/)), that's allowed, and
            will probably work today but may break in the future.

However, it's not allowed to put JavaScript or other content in docs published on docs.rs for the purpose of tracking visitors. For instance, adding Google Analytics scripts, tracking pixels, or site verification for services like Google Search Console. Crates that do this will have the relevant versions removed and may be blocked from docs.rs.

            Docs.rs is run and maintained by the [Docs.rs team](https://www.rust-lang.org/governance/teams/dev-tools#team-docs-rs).
            You can find us in #t-docs-rs on [Zulip](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/stream/356853-t-docs-rs).

---

# Builds

Source: https://docs.rs/about/builds

Docs.rs automatically builds documentation for crates released on [crates.io](https://crates.io/).
                It may take a while to build your crate, depending on how many crates are in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

                All crates are built in a sandbox using the nightly release of the Rust compiler.
                The current version in use is `rustc 1.98.0-nightly (4c9d2bfe4 2026-07-01)`.

                The README displayed on docs.rs follows Cargo’s `package.readme` rules.
                If `readme` is not set, docs.rs will look for `README.md`, `README.txt`, or `README` in the crate root.
                Set `readme = "path/to/file"` to use a custom file, `readme = true` to use `README.md`, or `readme = false` to disable the README.

                To recognize Docs.rs from your Rust code, you can test for the `docsrs` cfg, e.g.:

```
```
                To recognize Docs.rs from `build.rs` files, you can test for the environment variable `DOCS_RS`, e.g.:

`if var.is_ok `
              All targets other than `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` are cross-compiled. For implementation reasons, this is unlikely to change for the foreseeable future.

                You can configure how your crate is built by adding [package metadata](https://docs.rs/metadata) to your `Cargo.toml`, e.g.:

```
[]
 = ["--cfg", "my_cfg"]
```
`#[cfg(my_cfg)]` (not to be confused with `#[cfg(doc)]`) can be used for conditional compilation.
                This approach is also useful for setting
                When you start using docs.rs metadata or `#[cfg(docsrs)]` in your code, you might run into issues
                where your code builds fine locally but fails on docs.rs.
                To avoid this, you can add [ cargo docs-rs](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-docs-rs) to
                your test-suite.
                While it doesn't perfectly replicate our build environment, it can catch many common issues.

                The Docs.rs [README](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/blob/master/README.md#build-subcommand) describes how to build
                unpublished crate documentation locally using the same build environment as the Docs.rs build agent.

                Missing dependencies are a common reason for failed builds.
                Docs.rs dependencies are managed through
                [crates-build-env](https://github.com/rust-lang/crates-build-env).
                See [Forge](https://forge.rust-lang.org/docs-rs/add-dependencies.html) for how to add a dependency.

                Most of the sandbox is a read-only file system, including the source directory of your crate and its dependencies.
                If your `build.rs` generates files that are relevant for documentation, consider writing to the
                [cargo output directory](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/environment-variables.html#environment-variables-cargo-sets-for-crates),
                passed in the environment variable `OUT_DIR`.

All the builds are executed inside a sandbox with limited resources. The current limits are:

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |
| Maximum rustdoc execution time | 15m |
| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |
| Maximum number of build targets | 10 |

                If your build fails because it hit one of these limits, please
                [open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose)
                to get them increased for your crate.
                Since our build agent has finite resources, we have to consider each case individually. However, there are a few general policies:

If your crate fails to build for a reason not listed here, you can rebuild it from [crates.io](https://crates.io) website as you can see below:

Or you can [file an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues) if you think it's a **docs.rs** issue.

# Metadata

Source: https://docs.rs/about/metadata

You can customize docs.rs builds by defining `[package.metadata.docs.rs]`
		table in your crates' `Cargo.toml`.

The available configuration flags you can customize are:

```
[]
 = "test"
[]
# Features to pass to Cargo (default: [])
 = ["feature1", "feature2"]
# Whether to pass `--all-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Whether to pass `--no-default-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Target to test build on, used as the default landing page (default: "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu")
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
 = "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu"
# Targets to build (default: see below)
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
#
# Default targets:
# - x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - aarch64-apple-darwin
# - x86_64-pc-windows-msvc
# - aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - i686-pc-windows-msvc
#
# Set this to `[]` to only build the default target.
#
# If `default-target` is unset, the first element of `targets` is treated as the default target.
# Otherwise, these `targets` are built in addition to the default target.
# If both `default-target` and `targets` are unset,
#   all tier-one targets will be built and `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` will be used as the default target.
 = ["aarch64-apple-darwin", "x86_64-pc-windows-msvc"]
# If you want to instead add another target without overwriting the default ones:
 = ["i686-apple-darwin"]
# Additional `RUSTFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustc-arg"]
# Additional `RUSTDOCFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustdoc-arg"]
# List of command line arguments for `cargo`.
#
# These cannot be a subcommand, they may only be options.
 = ["-Z", "build-std"]
```

# Shorthand URLs

Source: https://docs.rs/about/redirections

Docs.rs uses semver to parse URLs. You can use this feature to access
            crates' documentation easily. Example of URL redirections for
            `clap` crate:

| URL | Redirects to documentation of |
|---|---|
| [docs.rs/clap](https://docs.rs/clap) | Latest version of clap |
| [docs.rs/clap::Command](https://docs.rs/clap::Command) | Latest version of clap, and search for "Command" within the crate |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2) | 2.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2.9](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2.9) | 2.9.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/2.9.3](https://docs.rs/clap/2.9.3) | 2.9.3 version (you don't need `=`unlike semver) |
| [docs.rs/clap/*](https://docs.rs/clap/*) | Latest version of this page (if it still exists). "latest" or "newest" work as well as `*`. |

---

# Download

Source: https://docs.rs/about/download

docs.rs stores the `rustdoc` output in a ZIP file.

                These archives can be used as a base for further processing of
                the documentation for offline readers like Dash or Zeal.
                **They are not directly usable for offline documentation.**

The download is possible for specific or semantic versions:

But also viaTo unpack the ZIP file you need any zip utility that supports PKZIP version 4.6 and BZIP2 & Deflate compression.

The archives will contain all the documentation HTML files for all targets and CSS/JS assets that are specific to the build. The default target will be found at the root, and other targets each in its own subfolder.

                Docs.rs is running rustdoc with `--static-root-path "/-/rustdoc.static/"`,
                which leads to all references to static assets breaking if they are not
                available under that path. Older builds used `--static-root-path "/"`, which
                means you will have to handle both.

                Since we're also adding `--emit=invocation-specific` to our build
                the archives will *not* contain any static assets that are specific to the
                toolchain. For now these will have to be downloaded file-by-file directly
                from docs.rs.

---

# Rustdoc JSON

Source: https://docs.rs/about/rustdoc-json

docs.rs builds & hosts the [ rustdoc JSON](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustdoc/unstable-features.html#json-output) output.

This structured version of the documentation can be used for inspecting the docs and types of the crate in a programmatic way.

                The JSON file you're downloading might have been built with an older version of `rustdoc`
                so you might have to check the `format_version` attribute to determine how to parse the structure.
                The [ rustdoc-types](https://docs.rs/rustdoc-types/) crate helps with this.

**
                We started building rustdoc JSON on 2025-05-23. So any release before that won't have a download
                available until our rebuilds reached that release.
            **

                The download URLs can be generic or specific, depending on what you need. In case of rebuilds we
                also keep old format versions around. **Until we rebuilt all releases, we might return
                a `404 NOT FOUND` for some.**

By default we use `zstd` compression, which is more space efficient and faster to decompress. For more limited environments we also started supporting `gzip` compression. You can receive gzip by adding `.gz` to the given URL.

Here some URL examples you can use.

| URL | Redirects to JSON download of |
|---|---|
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json) | latest version, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz) | latest version, default target, latest format-version, gzip compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42) | latest version, default target, format-version 42 |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json.zst](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json.zst) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version, zstd compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json) | latest version, windows target, latest format-version |

# overseerd_axum - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/overseerd-axum/0.9.1/overseerd_axum/

## Expand description

The Overseerd axum/HTTP protocol, built on the protocol-agnostic `overseerd-app` core.

This crate is a [ ProtocolPlugin](https://docs.rs/trait.ProtocolPlugin.html): it builds a real

[from](https://docs.rs/axum/0.8.9/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/axum/routing/struct.Router.html)

`axum::Router``#[controller]`
components, bridges the framework’s dependency injection into axum via the [extractor (so route handlers mix native axum extractors with DI), and serves over HTTP. Depend on it directly, or reach it through the](https://docs.rs/extract/struct.Inject.html)

`Inject``overseerd` facade’s `axum` feature.The DI bridge is deliberately thin and one-directional: nothing in `overseerd-di` or
`overseerd-core` knows axum exists. A per-request scope layer threads an
[ Arc<ScopeContainer>](https://docs.rs/overseerd-di/0.9.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/overseerd_di/container/struct.ScopeContainer.html) through the request extensions, and

[resolves components from it.](https://docs.rs/extract/struct.Inject.html)

# tatara_build_remote - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/tatara-build-remote/0.2.123/tatara_build_remote/

## Expand description

`tatara-build-remote` — layered Nix build transport for tatara guests.

Takes a `BuildRef` (flake + attr, raw Nix expression, store path, or
OCI image) and resolves it to a concrete `StorePath` using a
priority-ordered chain of transports. **First match wins.** Default
chain:

- **Attic cache**— pulls from a shared Attic instance (e.g.- `quero.lol`). Fastest path when the artifact is already cached.
- **ssh-ng remote builder**— submits to a remote Nix builder over- `ssh-ng://`. Used when Attic misses and the local machine can’t or shouldn’t build (cross-arch, resource constrained, etc.).
- **Local**—- `nix build`on the host. Last resort.

Any transport declared absent in the spec is skipped. If all declared
transports fail, `BuildError::AllTransportsFailed` bubbles up and
hospedeiro refuses to boot the guest — we fail closed.

[§](https://docs.rs#status)Status

**Phase H.5 landed.** `AtticTransport`, `SshRemoteTransport`, and
`LocalTransport` all ship in `transports.rs`.
`BuildTransportChain::to_layered()` composes them into a priority-
ordered `LayeredTransport` driven by `(defguest …)`’s `:build-on`
keyword.

[§](https://docs.rs#why-layered-not-single-target)Why layered, not single-target

The fleet at `quero.lol` has a shared Attic cache *and* an ssh-ng
builder pool. Cache hits are free; builds are expensive. Layering
lets the common case (pleme-io team members pulling pre-built
artifacts) skip the slow path entirely. Keys + SSH config come from
the cid node’s `pangea-builder.nix` — no new auth plumbing.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use transports::`- [AtticTransport](https://docs.rs/transports/struct.AtticTransport.html);
- `pub use transports::`- [LocalTransport](https://docs.rs/transports/struct.LocalTransport.html);
- `pub use transports::`- [SshRemoteTransport](https://docs.rs/transports/struct.SshRemoteTransport.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [transports](https://docs.rs/transports/index.html)
- Concrete `BuildTransport`implementations.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Build](https://docs.rs/struct.BuildTransportChain.html)- Transport - Chain
- Declarative transport chain. A `None`field means “don’t try this transport”.
- [Layered](https://docs.rs/struct.LayeredTransport.html)- Transport
- Layered transport — tries each child in order, returns the first success.
- [Store](https://docs.rs/struct.StorePath.html)- Path
- A Nix store path — content-addressed handle.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Build](https://docs.rs/enum.BuildError.html)- Error
- [Build](https://docs.rs/enum.BuildRef.html)- Ref
- A reference to something that becomes a Nix store path.

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

- [CRATE_](https://docs.rs/constant.CRATE_STATUS.html)- STATUS
- Phase marker. Bumped by each phase that lands a change.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Build](https://docs.rs/trait.BuildTransport.html)- Transport
- The operation-level transport trait. Phase H.5 implements
`AtticTransport`,`SshRemoteTransport`, and`LocalTransport`.

# overseerd_rpc_macros - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/overseerd-rpc-macros/0.9.1/overseerd_rpc_macros/

## Expand description

The Overseerd **RPC daemon** macros: `#[service]`, `#[handlers]`, `#[rpc]`, and
`app!`/`daemon!`. They are RPC-protocol-specific (they emit `::overseerd::daemon::*` types),
so they live in their own crate rather than the core `overseerd-macros`, built on the shared
[ overseerd_macros_core](https://docs.rs/overseerd-macros-core/0.9.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/overseerd_macros_core/index.html) codegen.

Re-exported through the `overseerd` facade’s `daemon` module; depend on the facade, not this
crate directly.

- `#[service]`is a- **router component**: a- `#[component]`(field-injected singleton) plus a service header, its- `{Service}Rpcs`slice, and the generated client struct.
- `#[handlers]`is- `MethodArgs<Rpcs>`— the base impl macro (- `#[methods]`:- `#[init]`+- `#[hook]`) plus the RPC extension, which registers each- `#[rpc]`method and contributes the client methods.
- `#[rpc]`marks a method inside a- `#[handlers]`impl (a marker stripped by- `#[handlers]`).

`app!`/`daemon!` are **not** here — they are protocol-agnostic core macros (in
`overseerd-macros`), selecting a protocol via a required `protocol:` field.

## Attribute Macros[§](https://docs.rs#attributes)

- [handlers](https://docs.rs/attr.handlers.html)
- Contributes the `#[rpc]`methods (and an optional`#[init]`/`#[hook]`s) of an inherent`impl`block to the service of`Self`.
- [rpc](https://docs.rs/attr.rpc.html)
- Marks a method inside a `#[handlers]`impl as an RPC. A**marker**consumed and stripped by`#[handlers]`; used on its own it emits a`compile_error!`.
- [service](https://docs.rs/attr.service.html)
- Declares a **service**— a router component exposing RPC methods.

# tatara_lisp_derive - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/tatara-lisp-derive/0.2.123/tatara_lisp_derive/

## Expand description

`#[derive(TataraDomain)]` — generate a `TataraDomain` impl from a Rust struct.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use tatara_lisp_derive::TataraDomain;
#[derive(TataraDomain)]
#[tatara(keyword = "defmonitor")]
pub struct MonitorSpec {
    pub name: String,
    pub query: String,
    pub threshold: f64,
    pub window_seconds: Option<i64>,
}
```
Generates:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
impl TataraDomain for MonitorSpec {
    const KEYWORD: &'static str = "defmonitor";
    fn compile_from_args(args: &[Sexp]) -> Result<Self> {
        let kw = parse_kwargs_strict(args, __TATARA_ALLOWED_KEYWORDS)?;
        Ok(Self {
            name: extract_string(&kw, "name")?.to_string(),
            query: extract_string(&kw, "query")?.to_string(),
            threshold: extract_float(&kw, "threshold")?,
            window_seconds: extract_optional_int(&kw, "window-seconds")?,
        })
    }
}
```
Invoked from Lisp:

`(defmonitor :name "prom-up" :query "up{…}" :threshold 0.99 :window-seconds 300)`Supported field types (v0):

- `String`,- `Option<String>`,- `Vec<String>`
- `i64`,- `i32`,- `u32`,- `usize`,- `u64`,- `Option<i64>`
- `f64`,- `f32`,- `Option<f64>`
- `bool`,- `Option<bool>`

## Derive Macros[§](https://docs.rs#derives)

- [Closed](https://docs.rs/derive.ClosedSet.html)- Set
- `#[derive(ClosedSet)]`— emit the substrate-wide [- `tatara_lisp::ClosedSet`] impl + the matching- `std::str::FromStr`- `ALL`+ projection +- `Unknown`+- `FromStr`shape).
- [Tatara](https://docs.rs/derive.TataraDomain.html)- Domain

# overseerd_client - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/overseerd-client/0.9.1/overseerd_client/

## Expand description

The Overseerd protocol-agnostic client *contract*.

The framework implements no client calls. It defines **capabilities** a protocol may
support — one trait each — and a protocol (`overseerd-rpc`, a future HTTP binding, …)
implements the subset it can. A protocol *declares* support by implementing a capability
and *refuses* by simply not: a client-streaming call over HTTP/1.1 is then a compile
error — a protocol limitation expressed in the type system, never a framework limit.

| Capability | trait | HTTP/1.1 | HTTP/2 | gRPC | custom RPC |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| one req → one resp | `Unary` | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| one req → many resp | `ServerStreaming` | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| many req → one resp | `ClientStreaming` | — | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| many req ↔ many resp | `BidiStreaming` | — | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |

The protocol owns **everything** behind each method: body encoding and parsing, framing,
routing, and streaming. A streaming capability returns the protocol’s own response
[ Stream](https://docs.rs/futures-core/0.3.32/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/futures_core/stream/trait.Stream.html) as an associated type — a real contract that the result

*is*a stream of decoded items, not an opaque box that would pretend any stream fits.

A generated client (`FooClient<C>`) bounds `C` on exactly the capabilities its RPCs need
and delegates to them, so the same generated code runs over any protocol providing those
capabilities.

The framework assumes **no serialization**: it never bounds a message on `serde` (a
protocol might use rkyv, protobuf, …). Instead a protocol declares what it can carry by
implementing [ Encodes<T>](https://docs.rs/trait.Encodes.html) /

[for those message types (typically a blanket](https://docs.rs/trait.Decodes.html)

`Decodes<T>``impl<T: Serialize> Encodes<T>`, or `impl<T: Archive> Encodes<T>`, …). A capability method
is bound `where Self: Encodes<Req> + Decodes<Resp>`, so a message the protocol cannot
serialize is a compile error — protocol-defined, never framework-assumed.## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Codec](https://docs.rs/struct.CodecError.html)- Error
- A body encode/decode failure. Carries a `StatusCode``BadInput`) and a human-readable message.
- [Error](https://docs.rs/struct.ErrorBody.html)- Body
- The client mirror of the server’s error response: a protocol-defined status `S`plus the raw error body bytes. The status is opaque to the framework (the protocol picks`S`; RPC uses its packed`transport::StatusCode`, HTTP uses`http::StatusCode`) — only the caller interprets it. The body is deserialized into`T`lazily and best-effort, so a body the handler serialized as a different type (or as raw, non-postcard bytes) degrades to a failed`deserialize`while`code`/`raw`stay usable.
- [Raw](https://docs.rs/struct.Raw.html)
- Marker for an error body whose payload type is not known statically (the generic call path). Typed clients substitute the method’s declared error type.
- [Stream](https://docs.rs/struct.StreamArg.html)- Arg
- A boxed input stream a streaming-request capability accepts. Build one from any `Stream`with`.into()`(or`new`

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Client](https://docs.rs/enum.ClientError.html)- Error
- Everything that can go wrong on a client call. Generic over the error body type `E`so typed clients surface an`ErrorBody<E>``deserialize``Raw`

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Bidi](https://docs.rs/trait.BidiStreaming.html)- Streaming
- A bidirectional stream of requests and responses (HTTP/2, gRPC, custom RPC — *not*HTTP/1.1). The request stream is pumped concurrently with reading the response stream.
- [Client](https://docs.rs/trait.ClientStreaming.html)- Streaming
- A stream of requests, one response (HTTP/2, gRPC, custom RPC — *not*HTTP/1.1, which has no streamed request body, so it does not implement this trait).
- [Decodes](https://docs.rs/trait.Decodes.html)
- A protocol can decode a `T`(a request, response, or stream item) from a wire body.
- [Encodes](https://docs.rs/trait.Encodes.html)
- A protocol can encode a `T`(a request, response, or stream item) into a wire body. Implemented by a protocol for the message types it supports.
- [Server](https://docs.rs/trait.ServerStreaming.html)- Streaming
- One request, a stream of responses (HTTP/1.1 chunked/SSE, HTTP/2, gRPC, custom RPC). The
response stream is the protocol’s own type — a contract that the result *is*a`Stream`
- [Transport](https://docs.rs/trait.Transport.html)
- The base every capability shares: a transport carries a protocol-defined `Status``transport::StatusCode`; HTTP sets it to`http::StatusCode`. Every capability requires this, so a transport declares its status once and it threads through every call shape’s errors.
- [Unary](https://docs.rs/trait.Unary.html)
- One request, one response. Every protocol supports this. The implementation owns body
encoding (via `Encodes``Decodes`

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [retype](https://docs.rs/fn.retype.html)
- Re-labels an untyped error onto a typed error of the same shape, preserving its status `S`. The only arm carrying`E`is`Remote`, whose body bytes are re-marked, not re-decoded. Used by protocol impls and generated clients.

# overseerd_transport - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/overseerd-transport/0.9.1/overseerd_transport/

## Expand description

Transport layer for Overseerd: the [ Transport](https://docs.rs/transport/trait.Transport.html)/

[/](https://docs.rs/transport/trait.Connection.html)

`Connection`[abstraction, the length-prefixed wire](https://docs.rs/transport/trait.Respond.html)

`Respond`[, and concrete transports (TCP, Unix sockets, in-memory).](https://docs.rs/protocol/index.html)

`protocol`The daemon is generic over [ Transport](https://docs.rs/transport/trait.Transport.html); a transport yields

[s, each of which yields](https://docs.rs/transport/trait.Connection.html)

`Connection``(IncomingCall, Responder)` pairs. Correlation ids live
entirely here — the daemon never sees them.Usually consumed through the `overseerd` facade crate.

# overseerd_app - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/overseerd-app/0.9.1/overseerd_app/

## Expand description

The Overseerd protocol-agnostic application core.

This crate ties the DI engine, config, hooks, and dirs into a runnable [ App](https://docs.rs/app/struct.App.html) that is
generic over the

[it installs. It owns the](https://docs.rs/protocol/trait.ProtocolPlugin.html)

`ProtocolPlugin`[, the agnostic](https://docs.rs/app/struct.AppBuilder.html)

`AppBuilder`[, scope planning, the lifecycle/serve envelope, the](https://docs.rs/registry/struct.AppRegistry.html)

`AppRegistry`[handle a protocol drives requests through, and the](https://docs.rs/runtime/struct.AppRuntime.html)

`AppRuntime`[/](https://docs.rs/protocol/trait.Plugin.html)

`Plugin`[/](https://docs.rs/protocol/trait.Protocol.html)

`Protocol`[seam.](https://docs.rs/protocol/trait.Serve.html)

`Serve`It is *protocol-agnostic*: it knows nothing of RPC, HTTP, or any wire format. A protocol
(the native RPC daemon, a future axum binding) is a sibling crate that implements these
traits over this foundation.

# overseerd_axum_macros - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/overseerd-axum-macros/0.9.1/overseerd_axum_macros/

## Expand description

The Overseerd **axum/HTTP controller** macros: `#[controller]`, `#[handlers]`, and the
route attributes (`#[get]`, `#[post]`, `#[put]`, `#[delete]`, `#[patch]`, `#[head]`,
`#[options]`, and the raw `#[route(METHOD, "/path")]`). They emit `::overseerd::web::*`
types, so they live in their own crate rather than the core `overseerd-macros`, built on
the shared [ overseerd_macros_core](https://docs.rs/overseerd-macros-core/0.9.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/overseerd_macros_core/index.html) codegen.

Re-exported through the `overseerd` facade’s `web` module; depend on the facade, not this
crate directly.

- `#[controller]`is a- **router component**: a- `#[component]`(field-injected singleton) plus a controller header, its- `{Controller}Routes`slice, and its- `ControllerDescriptor`.
- `#[handlers]`is- `MethodArgs<AxumHandlers>`— the base impl macro (- `#[methods]`:- `#[init]`- `#[hook]`) plus the route extension, which registers each route-attributed method.

- The route attributes mark a method inside a `#[handlers]`impl (stripped by`#[handlers]`).

## Attribute Macros[§](https://docs.rs#attributes)

- [controller](https://docs.rs/attr.controller.html)
- Declares a **controller**— a router component exposing HTTP routes.
- [delete](https://docs.rs/attr.delete.html)
- Marks a `DELETE`route inside a`#[handlers]`impl (see`get`
- [get](https://docs.rs/attr.get.html)
- Marks a `GET`route inside a`#[handlers]`impl. A marker consumed and stripped by`#[handlers]`; used on its own it emits a`compile_error!`.
- [handlers](https://docs.rs/attr.handlers.html)
- Contributes the route methods (and an optional `#[init]`/`#[hook]`s) of an inherent`impl`block to the controller of`Self`.
- [head](https://docs.rs/attr.head.html)
- Marks a `HEAD`route inside a`#[handlers]`impl (see`get`
- [message](https://docs.rs/attr.message.html)
- Marks a WebSocket message handler inside a `#[handlers]`impl of a`#[controller(ws = ..)]`:`#[message("destination")]`. A marker consumed and stripped by`#[handlers]`; used on its own it emits a`compile_error!`.
- [options](https://docs.rs/attr.options.html)
- Marks an `OPTIONS`route inside a`#[handlers]`impl (see`get`
- [patch](https://docs.rs/attr.patch.html)
- Marks a `PATCH`route inside a`#[handlers]`impl (see`get`
- [post](https://docs.rs/attr.post.html)
- Marks a `POST`route inside a`#[handlers]`impl (see`get`
- [put](https://docs.rs/attr.put.html)
- Marks a `PUT`route inside a`#[handlers]`impl (see`get`
- [route](https://docs.rs/attr.route.html)
- Marks a route by explicit method inside a `#[handlers]`impl:`#[route(METHOD, "/path")]`(see`get`
- [topics](https://docs.rs/attr.topics.html)
- Declares a **STOMP topic set**: an enum whose variants each carry a`#[topic("/topic/..")]`destination and a single payload type. Emits an`impl Topic`(typed server publish) and a`{Enum}Client<C>`with one`subscribe_<variant>()`per topic (typed client subscribe), so the same enum is the single source of truth for both sides. See the crate docs for an example.

                # RepoKai

A GitHub repository browser and manager with both a terminal UI and a desktop GUI.

## Features

- Browse your GitHub repositories with a 3-panel layout
- View README files, rendered: styled markdown with syntax-highlighted code blocks in the TUI, HTML in the GUI
- Mouse support in the TUI: wheel-scroll the panel under the cursor, click to focus and select
- View repo info: description, language, stars, visibility, last updated
- Publish a local git repo to GitHub
- Clone repos to your machine
- Edit repo description and visibility
- Open repos in your browser
- 4 visual themes: Dark, Light, 3.1 (retro DOS), TUI (Tokyo Night)

## Prerequisites

- **Git**must be installed and available in your PATH
- **GitHub authentication**is required. Either:- Set the `GITHUB_TOKEN`environment variable with a personal access token, or
- Log in with the [GitHub CLI](https://cli.github.com):`gh auth login`

- Set the

# taktora_connector_mqtt - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/taktora-connector-mqtt/0.1.0/taktora_connector_mqtt/

## Expand description

MQTT reference connector — M1 core (`BB_0036` / `FEAT_0036`).

This is the protocol-agnostic core of the MQTT connector, unit-testable
against an in-process mock. It carries **no** real MQTT backend and **no**
`Connector` impl — those land in later milestones (M2a/M3).

M1 modules:

- `topic`- `MqttTopic`/- `MqttTopicFilter`with publish/filter validation (- `REQ_0251`,- `REQ_0254`).
- `matcher`- `REQ_0254`, groundwork for the M2b demux,- `ADR_0129`).
- `routing`- `MqttRouting`,- `MqttQos`(- `REQ_0251`,- `REQ_0252`).
- `options`- `MqttConnectorOptions`typed builder with bounded bridge capacities (- `REQ_0259`).
- `health`- `MqttHealthMonitor`reusing the core- `HealthMonitor`with subscriber fan-out + inbound-drop latch (- `REQ_0261`).
- `session`- `MqttSessionLike`back-end seam.
- `mock`- `MockMqttSession`(always built).
- `bridge`- `OutboundBridge`/- `InboundBridge`with drop-accounting (- `REQ_0259`,- `REQ_0260`,- `REQ_0261`).

# overseerd_macros - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/overseerd-macros/0.9.1/overseerd_macros/

## Expand description

Procedural macros for the Overseerd framework.

These are re-exported from the `overseerd` facade crate; depend on that rather
than this crate directly. They span three subsystems — components (dependency
injection), services (RPC), and configuration.

| Macro | Applies to | Produces |
|---|---|---|
| `#[component]` | struct | `Component`impl + a factory (field-injection default,`factory = path`, or`default_factory = false`for a manual instance) |
| `#[service]` | struct | `Component`+`ServiceComponent`impls + a service header + a factory |
| `#[handlers]` | impl block | RPC handlers + RPC group |
| `#[methods]` | impl block | lifecycle methods — an `#[init]`constructor (an explicit factory) |
| `#[rpc]`/`#[init]` | method | markers consumed by `#[handlers]`/`#[methods]` |
| `#[injectable]` | trait | `Provide<dyn Trait>`impl (under`di-check`) |
| `#[config]` | struct/enum | `ConfigProperties`impl (with field`#[default = ".."]`templated defaults); auto-registers a binding when given`#[config(path = "..")]` |

[§](https://docs.rs#components-two-ways-to-provide-one)Components: two ways to provide one

A *component* is a singleton dependency, resolved by type. There are two ways
to get one into the daemon’s container:

- **System-constructed**— annotate the type with- `#[component]`(or a stateful- `#[service]`). The macro registers a factory; the container builds the instance from its dependencies during startup.
- **Manually provided**— construct the instance yourself and hand it to- `AppBuilder::with_component`. Annotate the type- `#[component(default_factory = false)]`, which emits the- `Component`metadata with no factory.

Both forms register a descriptor in the `DescriptorRegistry`; the difference
is whether the descriptor carries a factory or expects a provided instance.

[§](https://docs.rs#field-injection)Field injection

`#[component]` and `#[service]` build their factory by *field injection*. For
each field of the struct:

- an `Arc<T>`field is treated as a**dependency**and resolved from the container (`cx.resolve::<T>()`);
- a `Cfg<T>`field carrying`#[config("path")]`is a**config binding**resolved by property path (omit the path for the sole-binding shorthand);
- a `#[default]`field is**owned state**, built with`Default::default()`— so its type must implement`Default`, otherwise construct the component another way (an`#[init]`constructor, or`with_component`).

[§](https://docs.rs#implementation)Implementation

Each `#[proc_macro_*]` entry point here is a thin shim: it forwards its token streams to
the matching `expand` function in [ overseerd_macros_core](https://docs.rs/overseerd-macros-core/0.9.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/overseerd_macros_core/index.html), the ordinary library that
holds all the parsing and codegen (a proc-macro crate can only export proc-macros, so the
reusable machinery lives there). Errors are surfaced as

`compile_error!` by the core, not
by panicking.## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [app](https://docs.rs/macro.app.html)
- Assembles an app and validates it from one declaration.
- [daemon](https://docs.rs/macro.daemon.html)- Deprecated
- Deprecated alias for `app!`

## Attribute Macros[§](https://docs.rs#attributes)

- [component](https://docs.rs/attr.component.html)
- Declares a **system-constructed singleton component**on a struct.
- [config](https://docs.rs/attr.config.html)
- Implements the `ConfigProperties`trait for a config`struct`or`enum`, making it injectable as`Cfg<T>`from a property path.
- [injectable](https://docs.rs/attr.injectable.html)
- Marks a trait as injectable as `Arc<dyn Trait>`(providers register with`#[component(provide = dyn Trait)]`).
- [methods](https://docs.rs/attr.methods.html)
- Registers a component’s lifecycle methods from an inherent `impl`block.

# overseerd_config - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/overseerd-config/0.9.1/overseerd_config/

## Expand description

Configuration for the Overseerd framework.

Two layers live here. The **parser** is the format-agnostic core: a normalized
[ ConfigValue](https://docs.rs/enum.ConfigValue.html) tree, a placeholder grammar (

`${KEY}` / `${KEY:default}`), a
[chain, and a custom](https://docs.rs/trait.Resolver.html)

`Resolver`[deserializer that resolves placeholders](https://docs.rs/fn.from_value.html)

`from_value`*while*deserializing. The

**managed**layer (this crate’s

`managed` module) integrates
that parser with dependency injection: [injectables, the](https://docs.rs/struct.Cfg.html)

`Cfg<T>`[that loads and merges files, the](https://docs.rs/struct.ConfigManager.html)

`ConfigManager`[resolver the DI container reaches config through, and the two-phase](https://docs.rs/struct.ConfigStore.html)

`ConfigStore`[.](https://docs.rs/struct.ConfigReloader.html)

`ConfigReloader`The parser’s substitution failure type is [ TemplateError](https://docs.rs/enum.TemplateError.html); the managed layer’s
load/bind failure type is

[.](https://docs.rs/enum.ConfigError.html)

`ConfigError`## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use managed::`- [CONFIG_BINDINGS](https://docs.rs/static.CONFIG_BINDINGS.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [format](https://docs.rs/format/index.html)
- Source-format parsers that normalize into the shared `ConfigValue`

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Cfg](https://docs.rs/struct.Cfg.html)
- An injected configuration value, bound from a property path.
- [CfgNext](https://docs.rs/struct.CfgNext.html)
- A **proposed**configuration value handed to a`#[hook(ConfigReload)]`method during a reload, before it is committed. Read-only; derefs to`T`. If every hook accepts the proposal the value is committed into its`Cfg<T>`
- [Changed](https://docs.rs/struct.ChangedBinding.html)- Binding
- One binding changed by a reload.
- [Component](https://docs.rs/struct.ComponentHookReport.html)- Hook - Report
- One component’s config-reload hook outcome.
- [Config](https://docs.rs/struct.ConfigBinding.html)- Binding
- [Config](https://docs.rs/struct.ConfigBindingDescriptor.html)- Binding - Descriptor
- The link-time form of a `ConfigBinding``#[config(path = "..")]`so it is picked up by`ConfigManager::auto_discover``ConfigManager::with_config``Descriptor<ConfigBindingDescriptor>`.
- [Config](https://docs.rs/struct.ConfigManager.html)- Manager
- The merged configuration tree, owning the format it was read in.
- [Config](https://docs.rs/struct.ConfigReload.html)- Reload
- The config-reload hook kind: a `#[hook(ConfigReload)]`method runs when a config it targets is reloaded, receiving the proposed value(s) as`CfgNext<T>``HookOutcome`
- [Config](https://docs.rs/struct.ConfigReloadReport.html)- Reload - Report
- The outcome of a successful reload.
- [Config](https://docs.rs/struct.ConfigReloader.html)- Reloader
- A cheap, cloneable, injectable handle that re-reads configuration on demand.
- [Config](https://docs.rs/struct.ConfigStore.html)- Store
- A `Resolver``Cfg<T>`resolves through`ctx.get_resolver::<ConfigStore>()`rather than the component container. Bindings are deduped per`(type, path)`upstream, so the inner path map holds exactly one seed per path.
- [Config](https://docs.rs/struct.ConfigStr.html)- Str
- A string leaf decomposed into literal and placeholder segments.
- [Directories](https://docs.rs/struct.DirectoriesResolver.html)- Resolver
- A `config::Resolver``@`directory namespace.
- [Dynamic](https://docs.rs/struct.Dynamic.html)
- Reads every enabled format, letting the file extension decide the parser.
- [EnvResolver](https://docs.rs/struct.EnvResolver.html)
- Resolves keys from process environment variables.
- [MapResolver](https://docs.rs/struct.MapResolver.html)
- An explicit in-memory overlay, primarily for deterministic, env-free tests.
- [Placeholder](https://docs.rs/struct.Placeholder.html)
- A resolved-at-deserialize-time reference with an optional inline default.
- [Reload](https://docs.rs/struct.ReloadProposal.html)- Proposal
- The proposed configuration handed to config-reload hooks: the staged value of every
binding (changed bindings hold their newly-deserialized value, unchanged bindings hold
their current value), so a hook’s `CfgNext<T>`
- [Reload](https://docs.rs/struct.ReloadTriggers.html)- Triggers
- Which automatic reload triggers a `ConfigManager``ConfigReloader::reload``serve`/`run`and spawns the matching background tasks.
- [Resolve](https://docs.rs/struct.ResolveCtx.html)- Ctx
- Per-run resolution context: the root tree (for property-path references), the resolver chain, and an in-flight key stack for cycle detection.
- [Resolver](https://docs.rs/struct.ResolverChain.html)- Chain
- An ordered set of resolvers, consulted left to right.
- [Toml](https://docs.rs/struct.Toml.html)
- Reads only TOML (`application.toml`).
- [Value](https://docs.rs/struct.ValueDeserializer.html)- Deserializer
- A serde `Deserializer`over a single`ConfigValue`node.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Config](https://docs.rs/enum.ConfigError.html)- Error
- Errors from loading, merging, and binding configuration.
- [Config](https://docs.rs/enum.ConfigReloadError.html)- Reload - Error
- Errors from a configuration reload. On any error the live values are left untouched — a reload commits only when every changed binding re-binds and every affected hook accepts.
- [Config](https://docs.rs/enum.ConfigValue.html)- Value
- A format-agnostic configuration value tree.
- [Default](https://docs.rs/enum.DefaultSpec.html)- Spec
- The shape of a config type’s field defaults, emitted by the `#[config]`macro and consumed by the merge step.
- [EnumTag](https://docs.rs/enum.EnumTag.html)
- How an enum is tagged, so the merge can synthesize the same shape serde deserializes.
- [Format](https://docs.rs/enum.FormatId.html)- Id
- Which source format(s) a `ConfigManager``Format`type is erased.
- [Hook](https://docs.rs/enum.HookOutcome.html)- Outcome
- What a `#[hook(ConfigReload)]`hook reports back.`Err`from the hook aborts the reload; these variants all mean the proposal was accepted.
- [Segment](https://docs.rs/enum.Segment.html)
- One piece of a templated string.
- [Template](https://docs.rs/enum.TemplateError.html)- Error
- An error from config parsing, placeholder resolution, or typed deserialization.
- [Template](https://docs.rs/enum.TemplateErrorKind.html)- Error - Kind
- The specific failure, kept separate from path context so the same kind can be reported with or without a node path.

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

- [CONFIG_](https://docs.rs/constant.CONFIG_RELOADER_ID.html)- RELOADER_ - ID
- The stable component id of the seeded `ConfigReloader`
- [CONFIG_](https://docs.rs/constant.CONFIG_RELOADER_NAME.html)- RELOADER_ - NAME
- The display name of the seeded `ConfigReloader`

## Statics[§](https://docs.rs#statics)

- [CONFIG_](https://docs.rs/static.CONFIG_BINDINGS.html)- BINDINGS
- Link-time registry of every auto-registered config binding (a `#[config(path = "..")]`type), collected by`ConfigManager::auto_discover`

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Config](https://docs.rs/trait.ConfigDefaults.html)- Defaults
- Runtime, object-safe access to a config type’s `DefaultSpec`
- [Config](https://docs.rs/trait.ConfigProperties.html)- Properties
- A struct bindable from a configuration subtree, injectable as `Cfg<Self>`
- [Container](https://docs.rs/trait.ContainerConfigExt.html)- Config - Ext
- Ad-hoc config access from a built container: the relocated `.config()`accessor.
- [Format](https://docs.rs/trait.Format.html)
- A config source format: the file extensions it owns (and their parsers), in
precedence order. The type parameter on `ConfigManager``ConfigManager<Toml>`only try`.toml`while`ConfigManager<Dynamic>`tries all.
- [Reloadable](https://docs.rs/trait.ReloadableConfig.html)- Config
- A config binding the reloader can re-bind: it knows its path, how to re-deserialize its
type from a re-read tree, and how to stage its current value. Object-safe so the
reloader holds a `Vec<Box<dyn ReloadableConfig>>`across all bound types.
- [Resolver](https://docs.rs/trait.Resolver.html)
- Resolves a placeholder key to a raw string from one source (environment, an in-memory overlay, …).

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [from_](https://docs.rs/fn.from_value.html)- value
- Deserializes `T`from a`ConfigValue`
- [from_](https://docs.rs/fn.from_value_in.html)- value_ - in
- Like `from_value``value`(typically a subtree) while resolving placeholders against`root`(the full tree).
- [spawn_](https://docs.rs/fn.spawn_reload_triggers.html)- reload_ - triggers
- Spawns the background tasks for the requested triggers, returning their handles so the
caller can abort them on shutdown. Unsupported requests (SIGHUP off-Unix, watching
without the `watch`feature) are logged and skipped.

# xmlparser 0.13.6 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/xmlparser/0.13.6

## xmlparser

*xmlparser* is a low-level, pull-based, zero-allocation
[XML 1.0](https://www.w3.org/TR/xml/) parser.

### Example

```
for token in from
```
### Why a new library?

This library is basically a low-level XML tokenizer that preserves the positions of the tokens
and is not intended to be used directly.
If you are looking for a higher level solution, check out
[roxmltree](https://github.com/RazrFalcon/roxmltree).

### Benefits

- All tokens contain `StrSpan`structs which represent the position of the substring in the original document.
- Good error processing. All error types contain the position (line:column) where it occurred.
- No heap allocations.
- No dependencies.
- Tiny. ~1400 LOC and ~30KiB in the release build according to `cargo-bloat`.
- Supports `no_std`builds. To use without the standard library, disable the default features.

### Limitations

- Currently, only ENTITY objects are parsed from the DOCTYPE. All others are ignored.
- No tree structure validation. So an XML like `<root><child></root></child>`or a string without root element will be parsed without errors. You should check for this manually. On the other hand`<a/><a/>`will lead to an error.
- Duplicated attributes is not an error. So XML like `<item a="v1" a="v2"/>`will be parsed without errors. You should check for this manually.
- UTF-8 only.

### Safety

- The library must not panic. Any panic is considered a critical bug and should be reported.
- The library forbids unsafe code.

### License

Licensed under either of

- Apache License, Version 2.0
([LICENSE-APACHE](https://docs.rs/LICENSE-APACHE)or[http://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0](http://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0))
- MIT license
([LICENSE-MIT](https://docs.rs/LICENSE-MIT)or[http://opensource.org/licenses/MIT](http://opensource.org/licenses/MIT))

at your option.

### Contribution

Unless you explicitly state otherwise, any contribution intentionally submitted for inclusion in the work by you, as defined in the Apache-2.0 license, shall be dual licensed as above, without any additional terms or conditions.

# xmlparser - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/xmlparser/0.13.6/target-redirect/xmlparser/

## Expand description

*xmlparser* is a low-level, pull-based, zero-allocation
[XML 1.0](https://www.w3.org/TR/xml/) parser.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
for token in xmlparser::Tokenizer::from("<tagname name='value'/>") {
    println!("{:?}", token);
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#why-a-new-library)Why a new library?

This library is basically a low-level XML tokenizer that preserves the positions of the tokens
and is not intended to be used directly.
If you are looking for a higher level solution, check out
[roxmltree](https://github.com/RazrFalcon/roxmltree).

- No dependencies.
- Tiny. ~1400 LOC and ~30KiB in the release build according to `cargo-bloat`.
- Supports `no_std`builds. To use without the standard library, disable the default features.

[§](https://docs.rs#limitations)Limitations

- No tree structure validation. So an XML like `<root><child></root></child>`or a string without root element will be parsed without errors. You should check for this manually. On the other hand`<a/><a/>`will lead to an error.

[393](#393)    fn parse_next_impl(&mut self) -> Option<Result<Token<'a>>> {
[394](#394)        let s = &mut self.stream;
[395](#395)
[396](#396)        if s.at_end() {
[397](#397)            return None;
[398](#398)        }
[399](#399)
[400](#400)        let start = s.pos();
[401](#401)
[402](#402)        match self.state {
[403](#403)            State::Declaration => {
[404](#404)                self.state = State::AfterDeclaration;
[405](#405)                if s.starts_with(b"<?xml ") {
[406](#406)                    Some(Self::parse_declaration(s))
[407](#407)                } else {
[408](#408)                    None
[409](#409)                }
[410](#410)            }
[411](#411)            State::AfterDeclaration => {
[412](#412)                if s.starts_with(b"<!DOCTYPE") {
[413](#413)                    let t = Self::parse_doctype(s);
[414](#414)                    match t {
[415](#415)                        Ok(Token::DtdStart { .. }) => self.state = State::Dtd,
[416](#416)                        Ok(Token::EmptyDtd { .. }) => self.state = State::AfterDtd,
[417](#417)                        _ => {}
[418](#418)                    }
[419](#419)
[420](#420)                    Some(t)
[421](#421)                } else if s.starts_with(b"")))?;
[712](#712)        s.skip_string(b"-->")?;
[713](#713)
[714](#714)        if text.as_str().contains("--") {
[715](#715)            return Err(StreamError::InvalidCommentData);
[716](#716)        }
[717](#717)
[718](#718)        if text.as_str().ends_with('-') {
[719](#719)            return Err(StreamError::InvalidCommentEnd);
[720](#720)        }
[721](#721)
[722](#722)        let span = s.slice_back(start);
[723](#723)
[724](#724)        Ok(Token::Comment { text, span })
[725](#725)    }

[756](#756)    fn parse_doctype_impl(s: &mut Stream<'a>) -> StreamResult<Token<'a>> {
[758](#758)        let start = s.pos();
[759](#759)        s.advance(9);
[760](#760)
[761](#761)        s.consume_spaces()?;
[762](#762)        let name = s.consume_name()?;
[763](#763)        s.skip_spaces();
[764](#764)
[765](#765)        let external_id = Self::parse_external_id(s)?;
[766](#766)        s.skip_spaces();
[767](#767)
[768](#768)        let c = s.curr_byte()?;
[769](#769)        if c != b'[' && c !=  b'>' {
[770](#770)            static EXPECTED: &[u8] = &[b'[', b'>'];
[771](#771)            return Err(StreamError::InvalidCharMultiple(c, EXPECTED, s.gen_text_pos()));
[772](#772)        }
[773](#773)
[774](#774)        s.advance(1);
[775](#775)

[777](#777)        if c == b'[' {
[778](#778)            Ok(Token::DtdStart { name, external_id, span })
[779](#779)        } else {
[780](#780)            Ok(Token::EmptyDtd { name, external_id, span })
[781](#781)        }

[783](#783)
[784](#784)    fn parse_external_id(s: &mut Stream<'a>) -> StreamResult<Option<ExternalId<'a>>> {
[786](#786)        let v = if s.starts_with(b"SYSTEM") || s.starts_with(b"PUBLIC") {
[787](#787)            let start = s.pos();
[788](#788)            s.advance(6);
[789](#789)            let id = s.slice_back(start);
[790](#790)
[791](#791)            s.consume_spaces()?;
[792](#792)            let quote = s.consume_quote()?;
[793](#793)            let literal1 = s.consume_bytes(|_, c| c != quote);
[794](#794)            s.consume_byte(quote)?;
[795](#795)
[796](#796)            let v = if id.as_str() == "SYSTEM" {
[797](#797)                ExternalId::System(literal1)
[798](#798)            } else {
[799](#799)                s.consume_spaces()?;
[800](#800)                let quote = s.consume_quote()?;
[801](#801)                let literal2 = s.consume_bytes(|_, c| c != quote);
[802](#802)                s.consume_byte(quote)?;
[803](#803)
[804](#804)                ExternalId::Public(literal1, literal2)
[805](#805)            };
[806](#806)
[807](#807)            Some(v)
[808](#808)        } else {
[809](#809)            None
[810](#810)        };
[811](#811)
[812](#812)        Ok(v)
[813](#813)    }

[819](#819)    fn parse_entity_decl_impl(s: &mut Stream<'a>) -> StreamResult<Token<'a>> {

[827](#827)
[828](#828)        let is_ge = if s.try_consume_byte(b'%') {
[829](#829)            s.consume_spaces()?;
[830](#830)            false
[831](#831)        } else {
[832](#832)            true
[833](#833)        };
[834](#834)

[836](#836)        s.consume_spaces()?;
[837](#837)        let definition = Self::parse_entity_def(s, is_ge)?;
[838](#838)        s.skip_spaces();
[839](#839)        s.consume_byte(b'>')?;

[845](#845)
[846](#846)    fn parse_entity_def(s: &mut Stream<'a>, is_ge: bool) -> StreamResult<EntityDefinition<'a>> {
[853](#853)        let c = s.curr_byte()?;
[854](#854)        match c {
[855](#855)            b'"' | b'\'' => {
[856](#856)                let quote = s.consume_quote()?;
[857](#857)                let value = s.consume_bytes(|_, c| c != quote);
[858](#858)                s.consume_byte(quote)?;
[859](#859)
[860](#860)                Ok(EntityDefinition::EntityValue(value))
[861](#861)            }
[862](#862)            b'S' | b'P' => {
[863](#863)                if let Some(id) = Self::parse_external_id(s)? {
[864](#864)                    if is_ge {
[865](#865)                        s.skip_spaces();
[866](#866)                        if s.starts_with(b"NDATA") {
[867](#867)                            s.advance(5);
[868](#868)                            s.consume_spaces()?;
[869](#869)                            s.skip_name()?;
[870](#870)                            }
[872](#872)                    }
[873](#873)
[874](#874)                    Ok(EntityDefinition::ExternalId(id))
[875](#875)                } else {
[876](#876)                    Err(StreamError::InvalidExternalID)
[877](#877)                }
[878](#878)            }
[879](#879)            _ => {
[880](#880)                static EXPECTED: &[u8] = &[b'"', b'\'', b'S', b'P'];
[881](#881)                let pos = s.gen_text_pos();
[882](#882)                Err(StreamError::InvalidCharMultiple(c, EXPECTED, pos))
[883](#883)            }
[884](#884)        }
[885](#885)    }
[886](#886)
[887](#887)    fn consume_decl(s: &mut Stream) -> StreamResult<()> {
[888](#888)        s.skip_bytes(|_, c| c != b'>');
[889](#889)        s.consume_byte(b'>')?;
[890](#890)        Ok(())
[891](#891)    }

[928](#928)    fn parse_close_element_impl(s: &mut Stream<'a>) -> StreamResult<Token<'a>> {

[941](#941)
[942](#942)    fn parse_attribute(s: &mut Stream<'a>) -> StreamResult<Token<'a>> {
[944](#944)        let attr_start = s.pos();
[945](#945)        let has_space = s.starts_with_space();
[946](#946)        s.skip_spaces();
[947](#947)
[948](#948)        if let Ok(c) = s.curr_byte() {
[949](#949)            let start = s.pos();
[950](#950)
[951](#951)            match c {
[952](#952)                b'/' => {
[953](#953)                    s.advance(1);
[954](#954)                    s.consume_byte(b'>')?;
[955](#955)                    let span = s.slice_back(start);
[956](#956)                    return Ok(Token::ElementEnd { end: ElementEnd::Empty, span });
[957](#957)                }
[958](#958)                b'>' => {
[959](#959)                    s.advance(1);
[960](#960)                    let span = s.slice_back(start);
[961](#961)                    return Ok(Token::ElementEnd { end: ElementEnd::Open, span });
[962](#962)                }
[963](#963)                _ => {}
[964](#964)            }
[965](#965)        }
[966](#966)
[967](#967)        if !has_space {
[968](#968)            if !s.at_end() {
[969](#969)                return Err(StreamError::InvalidSpace(
[970](#970)                    s.curr_byte_unchecked(), s.gen_text_pos_from(attr_start))
[971](#971)                );
[972](#972)            } else {
[973](#973)                return Err(StreamError::UnexpectedEndOfStream);
[974](#974)            }
[975](#975)        }
[976](#976)
[977](#977)        let start = s.pos();
[978](#978)
[979](#979)        let (prefix, local) = s.consume_qname()?;
[980](#980)        s.consume_eq()?;
[981](#981)        let quote = s.consume_quote()?;
[982](#982)        let quote_c = quote as char;
[983](#983)        let value = s.consume_chars(|_, c| c != quote_c && c != '<')?;
[985](#985)        s.consume_byte(quote)?;
[986](#986)        let span = s.slice_back(start);
[987](#987)
[988](#988)        Ok(Token::Attribute { prefix, local, value, span })
[989](#989)    }
[990](#990)
[991](#991)    fn parse_text(s: &mut Stream<'a>) -> Result<Token<'a>> {
[992](#992)        map_err_at!(Self::parse_text_impl(s), s, InvalidCharData)
[993](#993)    }
[994](#994)
[995](#995)    fn parse_text_impl(s: &mut Stream<'a>) -> StreamResult<Token<'a>> {
[996](#996)        let text = s.consume_chars(|_, c| c != '<')?;
[997](#997)
[998](#998)        if text.as_str().contains('>') {
[1003](#1003)            if text.as_str().contains("]]>") {
[1004](#1004)                return Err(StreamError::InvalidCharacterData);
[1005](#1005)            }
[1006](#1006)        }
[1007](#1007)
[1008](#1008)        Ok(Token::Text { text })
[1009](#1009)    }
[1010](#1010)
[1011](#1011)    pub fn stream(&self) -> Stream<'a> {
[1013](#1013)        self.stream
[1014](#1014)    }
[1015](#1015)}
[1016](#1016)
[1017](#1017)impl<'a> Iterator for Tokenizer<'a> {
[1018](#1018)    type Item = Result<Token<'a>>;
[1019](#1019)
[1020](#1020)    #[inline]
[1021](#1021)    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<Self::Item> {
[1022](#1022)        let mut t = None;
[1023](#1023)        while !self.stream.at_end() && self.state != State::End && t.is_none() {
[1024](#1024)            t = self.parse_next_impl();
[1025](#1025)        }
[1026](#1026)
[1027](#1027)        if let Some(Err(_)) = t {
[1028](#1028)            self.stream.jump_to_end();
[1029](#1029)            self.state = State::End;
[1030](#1030)        }
[1031](#1031)
[1032](#1032)        t
[1033](#1033)    }
[1034](#1034)}

# StrSpan in xmlparser - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/xmlparser/0.13.6/xmlparser/struct.StrSpan.html

`pub struct StrSpan<'a> { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

A string slice.

Like `&str`, but also contains the position in the input XML
from which it was parsed.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

1.9.0 · [Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/src/core/str/mod.rs.html#373)#### pub fn [is_char_boundary](https://docs.rs#method.is_char_boundary)(&self, index: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/src/core/str/mod.rs.html#373)

#### pub fn [is_char_boundary](https://docs.rs#method.is_char_boundary)(&self, index: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)

Checks that `index`-th byte is the first byte in a UTF-8 code point
sequence or the end of the string.

The start and end of the string (when `index == self.len()`) are
considered to be boundaries.

Returns `false` if `index` is greater than `self.len()`.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-2)Examples

```
let s = "Löwe 老虎 Léopard";
assert!(s.is_char_boundary(0));
// start of `老`
assert!(s.is_char_boundary(6));
assert!(s.is_char_boundary(s.len()));
// second byte of `ö`
assert!(!s.is_char_boundary(2));
// third byte of `老`
assert!(!s.is_char_boundary(8));
```
1.91.0 · [Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/src/core/str/mod.rs.html#422)#### pub fn [floor_char_boundary](https://docs.rs#method.floor_char_boundary)(&self, index: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)) -> [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/src/core/str/mod.rs.html#422)

#### pub fn [floor_char_boundary](https://docs.rs#method.floor_char_boundary)(&self, index: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)) -> [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)

Finds the closest `x` not exceeding `index` where [ is_char_boundary(x)](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html#method.is_char_boundary) is

`true`.This method can help you truncate a string so that it’s still valid UTF-8, but doesn’t exceed a given number of bytes. Note that this is done purely at the character level and can still visually split graphemes, even though the underlying characters aren’t split. For example, the emoji 🧑🔬 (scientist) could be split so that the string only includes 🧑 (person) instead.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-3)Examples

```
let s = "❤️🧡💛💚💙💜";
assert_eq!(s.len(), 26);
assert!(!s.is_char_boundary(13));
let closest = s.floor_char_boundary(13);
assert_eq!(closest, 10);
assert_eq!(&s[..closest], "❤️🧡");
```

Converts a string slice to a raw pointer.

As string slices are a slice of bytes, the raw pointer points to a
[ u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html). This pointer will be pointing to the first byte of the string
slice.

The caller must ensure that the returned pointer is never written to.
If you need to mutate the contents of the string slice, use [ as_mut_ptr](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html#method.as_mut_ptr).

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-6)Examples

```
let s = "Hello";
let ptr = s.as_ptr();
```
Returns a subslice of `str`.

This is the non-panicking alternative to indexing the `str`. Returns
[ None](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html#variant.None) whenever equivalent indexing operation would panic.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-7)Examples

```
let v = String::from("🗻∈🌏");
assert_eq!(Some("🗻"), v.get(0..4));
// indices not on UTF-8 sequence boundaries
assert!(v.get(1..).is_none());
assert!(v.get(..8).is_none());
// out of bounds
assert!(v.get(..42).is_none());
```
1.20.0 · [Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/src/core/str/mod.rs.html#684)#### pub unsafe fn [get_unchecked](https://docs.rs#method.get_unchecked)<I>(&self, i: I) -> &<I as [SliceIndex](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/slice/index/trait.SliceIndex.html)<[str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html)>>::[Output](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/slice/index/trait.SliceIndex.html#associatedtype.Output)

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/src/core/str/mod.rs.html#684)

#### pub unsafe fn [get_unchecked](https://docs.rs#method.get_unchecked)<I>(&self, i: I) -> &<I as [SliceIndex](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/slice/index/trait.SliceIndex.html)<[str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html)>>::[Output](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/slice/index/trait.SliceIndex.html#associatedtype.Output)

Returns an unchecked subslice of `str`.

This is the unchecked alternative to indexing the `str`.

[§](https://docs.rs#safety)Safety

Callers of this function are responsible that these preconditions are satisfied:

- The starting index must not exceed the ending index;
- Indexes must be within bounds of the original slice;
- Indexes must lie on UTF-8 sequence boundaries.

Failing that, the returned string slice may reference invalid memory or
violate the invariants communicated by the `str` type.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-8)Examples

```
let v = "🗻∈🌏";
unsafe {
    assert_eq!("🗻", v.get_unchecked(0..4));
    assert_eq!("∈", v.get_unchecked(4..7));
    assert_eq!("🌏", v.get_unchecked(7..11));
}
```

#### pub unsafe fn [slice_unchecked](https://docs.rs#method.slice_unchecked)(&self, begin: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html), end: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)) -> &[str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html)

Creates a string slice from another string slice, bypassing safety checks.

This is generally not recommended, use with caution! For a safe
alternative see [ str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html) and

[.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/index/trait.Index.html)

`Index`This new slice goes from `begin` to `end`, including `begin` but
excluding `end`.

To get a mutable string slice instead, see the
[ slice_mut_unchecked](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html#method.slice_mut_unchecked) method.

[§](https://docs.rs#safety-1)Safety

Callers of this function are responsible that three preconditions are satisfied:

- `begin`must not exceed- `end`.
- `begin`and- `end`must be byte positions within the string slice.
- `begin`and- `end`must lie on UTF-8 sequence boundaries.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-9)Examples

```
let s = "Löwe 老虎 Léopard";

    assert_eq!("Löwe 老虎 Léopard", s.slice_unchecked(0, 21));
}
let s = "Hello, world!";
unsafe {
    assert_eq!("world", s.slice_unchecked(7, 12));
}
```
Divides one string slice into two at an index.

The argument, `mid`, should be a byte offset from the start of the
string. It must also be on the boundary of a UTF-8 code point.

The two slices returned go from the start of the string slice to `mid`,
and from `mid` to the end of the string slice.

To get mutable string slices instead, see the [ split_at_mut](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html#method.split_at_mut)
method.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics)Panics

Panics if `mid` is not on a UTF-8 code point boundary, or if it is past
the end of the last code point of the string slice.  For a non-panicking
alternative see [ split_at_checked](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html#method.split_at_checked).

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-10)Examples

```
let s = "Per Martin-Löf";
let (first, last) = s.split_at(3);
assert_eq!("Per", first);
assert_eq!(" Martin-Löf", last);
```
Divides one string slice into two at an index.

The argument, `mid`, should be a valid byte offset from the start of the
string. It must also be on the boundary of a UTF-8 code point. The
method returns `None` if that’s not the case.

The two slices returned go from the start of the string slice to `mid`,
and from `mid` to the end of the string slice.

To get mutable string slices instead, see the [ split_at_mut_checked](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html#method.split_at_mut_checked)
method.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-11)Examples

```
let s = "Per Martin-Löf";
let (first, last) = s.split_at_checked(3).unwrap();
assert_eq!("Per", first);
assert_eq!(" Martin-Löf", last);
assert_eq!(None, s.split_at_checked(13));  // Inside “ö”
assert_eq!(None, s.split_at_checked(16));  // Beyond the string length
```
Returns an iterator over the [ char](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.char.html)s of a string slice.

As a string slice consists of valid UTF-8, we can iterate through a
string slice by [ char](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.char.html). This method returns such an iterator.

It’s important to remember that [ char](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.char.html) represents a Unicode Scalar
Value, and might not match your idea of what a ‘character’ is. Iteration
over grapheme clusters may be what you actually want. This functionality
is not provided by Rust’s standard library, check crates.io instead.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-12)Examples

Basic usage:

```
let word = "goodbye";
let count = word.chars().count();
assert_eq!(7, count);
let mut chars = word.chars();
assert_eq!(Some('g'), chars.next());
assert_eq!(Some('o'), chars.next());
assert_eq!(Some('o'), chars.next());
assert_eq!(Some('d'), chars.next());
assert_eq!(Some('b'), chars.next());
assert_eq!(Some('y'), chars.next());
assert_eq!(Some('e'), chars.next());
assert_eq!(None, chars.next());
```
Remember, [ char](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.char.html)s might not match your intuition about characters:

```
let y = "y̆";
let mut chars = y.chars();
assert_eq!(Some('y'), chars.next()); // not 'y̆'
assert_eq!(Some('\u{0306}'), chars.next());
assert_eq!(None, chars.next());
```

#### pub fn [char_indices](https://docs.rs#method.char_indices)(&self) -> [CharIndices](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/str/iter/struct.CharIndices.html)<'_>

Returns an iterator over the [ char](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.char.html)s of a string slice, and their
positions.

As a string slice consists of valid UTF-8, we can iterate through a
string slice by [ char](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.char.html). This method returns an iterator of both
these

[s, as well as their byte positions.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.char.html)

`char`The iterator yields tuples. The position is first, the [ char](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.char.html) is
second.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-13)Examples

Basic usage:

```
let word = "goodbye";
let count = word.char_indices().count();
assert_eq!(7, count);
let mut char_indices = word.char_indices();
assert_eq!(Some((0, 'g')), char_indices.next());
assert_eq!(Some((1, 'o')), char_indices.next());
assert_eq!(Some((2, 'o')), char_indices.next());
assert_eq!(Some((3, 'd')), char_indices.next());
assert_eq!(Some((4, 'b')), char_indices.next());
assert_eq!(Some((5, 'y')), char_indices.next());
assert_eq!(Some((6, 'e')), char_indices.next());
assert_eq!(None, char_indices.next());
```
Remember, [ char](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.char.html)s might not match your intuition about characters:

```
let yes = "y̆es";
let mut char_indices = yes.char_indices();
assert_eq!(Some((0, 'y')), char_indices.next()); // not (0, 'y̆')
assert_eq!(Some((1, '\u{0306}')), char_indices.next());
// note the 3 here - the previous character took up two bytes
assert_eq!(Some((3, 'e')), char_indices.next());
assert_eq!(Some((4, 's')), char_indices.next());
assert_eq!(None, char_indices.next());
```
Returns an iterator over the bytes of a string slice.

As a string slice consists of a sequence of bytes, we can iterate through a string slice by byte. This method returns such an iterator.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-14)Examples

```
let mut bytes = "bors".bytes();
assert_eq!(Some(b'b'), bytes.next());
assert_eq!(Some(b'o'), bytes.next());
assert_eq!(Some(b'r'), bytes.next());
assert_eq!(Some(b's'), bytes.next());
assert_eq!(None, bytes.next());
```
1.1.0 · [Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/src/core/str/mod.rs.html#1195)#### pub fn [split_whitespace](https://docs.rs#method.split_whitespace)(&self) -> [SplitWhitespace](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/str/iter/struct.SplitWhitespace.html)<'_>

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/src/core/str/mod.rs.html#1195)

#### pub fn [split_whitespace](https://docs.rs#method.split_whitespace)(&self) -> [SplitWhitespace](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/str/iter/struct.SplitWhitespace.html)<'_>

Splits a string slice by whitespace.

The iterator returned will return string slices that are sub-slices of the original string slice, separated by any amount of whitespace.

‘Whitespace’ is defined according to the terms of the Unicode Derived
Core Property `White_Space`. If you only want to split on ASCII whitespace
instead, use [ split_ascii_whitespace](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html#method.split_ascii_whitespace).

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-15)Examples

Basic usage:

```
let mut iter = "A few words".split_whitespace();
assert_eq!(Some("A"), iter.next());
assert_eq!(Some("few"), iter.next());
assert_eq!(Some("words"), iter.next());
assert_eq!(None, iter.next());
```
All kinds of whitespace are considered:

```
let mut iter = " Mary   had\ta\u{2009}little  \n\t lamb".split_whitespace();
assert_eq!(Some("Mary"), iter.next());
assert_eq!(Some("had"), iter.next());
assert_eq!(Some("a"), iter.next());
assert_eq!(Some("little"), iter.next());
assert_eq!(Some("lamb"), iter.next());
assert_eq!(None, iter.next());
```
If the string is empty or all whitespace, the iterator yields no string slices:

```
assert_eq!("".split_whitespace().next(), None);
assert_eq!("   ".split_whitespace().next(), None);
```
1.34.0 · [Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/src/core/str/mod.rs.html#1249)#### pub fn [split_ascii_whitespace](https://docs.rs#method.split_ascii_whitespace)(&self) -> [SplitAsciiWhitespace](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/str/iter/struct.SplitAsciiWhitespace.html)<'_>

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/src/core/str/mod.rs.html#1249)

#### pub fn [split_ascii_whitespace](https://docs.rs#method.split_ascii_whitespace)(&self) -> [SplitAsciiWhitespace](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/str/iter/struct.SplitAsciiWhitespace.html)<'_>

Splits a string slice by ASCII whitespace.

The iterator returned will return string slices that are sub-slices of the original string slice, separated by any amount of ASCII whitespace.

This uses the same definition as [ char::is_ascii_whitespace](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.char.html#method.is_ascii_whitespace).
To split by Unicode

`Whitespace` instead, use [. Note that because of this difference in definition, even if](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html#method.split_whitespace)

`split_whitespace``s.is_ascii()`
is `true`, `s.split_ascii_whitespace()` behavior will differ from `s.split_whitespace()`
if `s` contains U+000B VERTICAL TAB.[§](https://docs.rs#examples-16)Examples

let mut iter = " Mary   had\ta little  \n\t lamb".split_ascii_whitespace();
assert_eq!(Some("Mary"), iter.next());
