# http - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/http/1.4.2/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/http/index.html

## Expand description

A general purpose library of common HTTP types

This crate is a general purpose library for common types found when working
with the HTTP protocol. You’ll find [ Request](https://docs.rs/request/struct.Request.html) and

[types for working as either a client or a server as well as all of their components. Notably you’ll find](https://docs.rs/response/struct.Response.html)

`Response``Uri` for what a [is requesting, a](https://docs.rs/request/struct.Request.html)

`Request`[for how it’s being requested, a](https://docs.rs/method/struct.Method.html)

`Method`[for what sort of response came back, a](https://docs.rs/status/struct.StatusCode.html)

`StatusCode`[for how this was communicated, and](https://docs.rs/version/struct.Version.html)

`Version`[/](https://docs.rs/header/struct.HeaderName.html)

`HeaderName`[definitions to get grouped in a](https://docs.rs/header/struct.HeaderValue.html)

`HeaderValue`[to work with request/response headers.](https://docs.rs/header/struct.HeaderMap.html)

`HeaderMap`You will notably *not* find an implementation of sending requests or
spinning up a server in this crate. It’s intended that this crate is the
“standard library” for HTTP clients and servers without dictating any
particular implementation.

[§](https://docs.rs#requests-and-responses)Requests and Responses

Perhaps the main two types in this crate are the [ Request](https://docs.rs/request/struct.Request.html) and

[types. A](https://docs.rs/response/struct.Response.html)

`Response`[could either be constructed to get sent off as a client or it can also be received to generate a](https://docs.rs/request/struct.Request.html)

`Request`[for a server. Similarly as a client a](https://docs.rs/response/struct.Response.html)

`Response`[is what you get after sending a](https://docs.rs/response/struct.Response.html)

`Response`[, whereas on a server you’ll be manufacturing a](https://docs.rs/request/struct.Request.html)

`Request`[to send back to the client.](https://docs.rs/response/struct.Response.html)

`Response`Each type has a number of accessors for the component fields. For as a server you might want to inspect a requests URI to dispatch it:

```
use http::{Request, Response};
fn response(req: Request<()>) -> http::Result<Response<()>> {
    match req.uri().path() {
        "/" => index(req),
        "/foo" => foo(req),
        "/bar" => bar(req),
        _ => not_found(req),
    }
}
```
On a [ Request](https://docs.rs/request/struct.Request.html) you’ll also find accessors like

[to return a](https://docs.rs/request/struct.Request.html#method.method)

`method`[and](https://docs.rs/method/struct.Method.html)

`Method`[to inspect the various headers. A](https://docs.rs/request/struct.Request.html#method.method)

`headers`[has similar methods for headers, the status code, etc.](https://docs.rs/response/struct.Response.html)

`Response`In addition to getters, request/response types also have mutable accessors to edit the request/response:

```
use http::{HeaderValue, Response, StatusCode};
use http::header::CONTENT_TYPE;
fn add_server_headers<T>(response: &mut Response<T>) {
    response.headers_mut()
        .insert(CONTENT_TYPE, HeaderValue::from_static("text/html"));
    *response.status_mut() = StatusCode::OK;
}
```
And finally, one of the most important aspects of requests/responses, the
body! The [ Request](https://docs.rs/request/struct.Request.html) and

[types in this crate are](https://docs.rs/response/struct.Response.html)

`Response`*generic*in what their body is. This allows downstream libraries to use different representations such as

`Request<Vec<u8>>`, `Response<impl Read>`,
`Request<impl Stream<Item = Vec<u8>, Error = _>>`, or even
`Response<MyCustomType>` where the custom type was deserialized from JSON.The body representation is intentionally flexible to give downstream libraries maximal flexibility in implementing the body as appropriate.

[§](https://docs.rs#http-headers)HTTP Headers

Another major piece of functionality in this library is HTTP header
interpretation and generation. The `HeaderName` type serves as a way to
define header *names*, or what’s to the left of the colon. A `HeaderValue`
conversely is the header *value*, or what’s to the right of a colon.

For example, if you have an HTTP request that looks like:

```
GET /foo HTTP/1.1
Accept: text/html
```
Then `"Accept"` is a [ HeaderName](https://docs.rs/header/struct.HeaderName.html) while

`"text/html"` is a [. Each of these is a dedicated type to allow for a number of interesting optimizations and to also encode the static guarantees of each type. For example a](https://docs.rs/header/struct.HeaderValue.html)

`HeaderValue`[is always a valid](https://docs.rs/header/struct.HeaderName.html)

`HeaderName``&str`, but a [may not be valid UTF-8.](https://docs.rs/header/struct.HeaderValue.html)

`HeaderValue`The most common header names are already defined for you as constant values
in the [ header](https://docs.rs/header/index.html) module of this crate. For example:

```
use http::header::{self, HeaderName};
let name: HeaderName = header::ACCEPT;
assert_eq!(name.as_str(), "accept");
```
You can, however, also parse header names from strings:

```
use http::header::{self, HeaderName};
let name = "Accept".parse::<HeaderName>().unwrap();
assert_eq!(name, header::ACCEPT);
```
Header values can be created from string literals through the [ from_static](https://docs.rs/header/struct.HeaderValue.html#method.from_static)
function:

```
use http::HeaderValue;
let value = HeaderValue::from_static("text/html");
assert_eq!(value.as_bytes(), b"text/html");
```
And header values can also be parsed like names:

```
use http::HeaderValue;
let value = "text/html";
let value = value.parse::<HeaderValue>().unwrap();
```
Most HTTP requests and responses tend to come with more than one header, so
it’s not too useful to just work with names and values only! This crate also
provides a [ HeaderMap](https://docs.rs/header/struct.HeaderMap.html) type which is a specialized hash map for keys as

[and generic values. This type, like header names, is optimized for common usage but should continue to scale with your needs over time.](https://docs.rs/header/struct.HeaderName.html)

`HeaderName`[§](https://docs.rs#uris)URIs

Each HTTP [ Request](https://docs.rs/request/struct.Request.html) has an associated URI with it. This may just be a path
like

`/index.html` but it could also be an absolute URL such as
`https://www.rust-lang.org/index.html`. A [has a number of accessors to interpret it:](https://docs.rs/uri/struct.Uri.html)

`URI````
use http::Uri;
use http::uri::Scheme;
let uri = "https://www.rust-lang.org/index.html".parse::<Uri>().unwrap();
assert_eq!(uri.scheme(), Some(&Scheme::HTTPS));
assert_eq!(uri.host(), Some("www.rust-lang.org"));
assert_eq!(uri.path(), "/index.html");
assert_eq!(uri.query(), None);
```
## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

# overseerd_axum::controller - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/overseerd-axum/0.9.1/overseerd_axum/controller/index.html

## Expand description

Controllers: the HTTP-facing services, and how they register their routes.

A controller is a DI singleton (like an RPC service) annotated with `#[controller]`. Its
`#[handlers]` impl blocks contribute routes. The macro emits a [ ControllerDescriptor](https://docs.rs/struct.ControllerDescriptor.html)
into the

[slice and an implementation of](https://docs.rs/static.CONTROLLERS.html)

`CONTROLLERS`[; the](https://docs.rs/trait.Controller.html)

`Controller`[folds the slice on](https://docs.rs/plugin/struct.AxumPlugin.html)

`AxumPlugin``auto_discover` and merges each
controller’s [when the protocol is built.](https://docs.rs/axum/0.8.9/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/axum/routing/struct.Router.html)

`axum::Router`## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Controller](https://docs.rs/struct.ControllerDescriptor.html)- Descriptor
- A controller’s link-time registration: its identity and a builder for its routes.

## Statics[§](https://docs.rs#statics)

- [CONTROLLERS](https://docs.rs/static.CONTROLLERS.html)
- The link-time slice every `#[controller]`registers into, mirroring the RPC`SERVICES`slice.`AxumPlugin::auto_discover`

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Controller](https://docs.rs/trait.Controller.html)
- Implemented by every `#[controller]`struct: the base path and a builder for its routes.

# overseerd_axum::extract - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/overseerd-axum/0.9.1/overseerd_axum/extract/index.html

## Expand description

The DI↔axum bridge: a per-request scope handle and the [ Inject](https://docs.rs/struct.Inject.html) extractor.

The integration surface between the framework’s dependency injection and axum is a
single [ ScopeHandle](https://docs.rs/struct.ScopeHandle.html) — an

`Arc` of the request’s
[— carried in the request’s](https://docs.rs/overseerd-di/0.9.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/overseerd_di/container/struct.ScopeContainer.html)

`ScopeContainer`[. The protocol’s scope layer opens the request scope and inserts the handle;](https://docs.rs/http/1.4.2/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/http/extensions/struct.Extensions.html)

`Extensions`[reads it back out and resolves a component through the scope chain. Native axum extractors (](https://docs.rs/struct.Inject.html)

`Inject``Json`, `Path`, `Query`, `State`, …)
are untouched and compose with [in the same handler signature.](https://docs.rs/struct.Inject.html)

`Inject`## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Inject](https://docs.rs/struct.Inject.html)
- Injects anything a constructor parameter can be — any `FromContainer``Arc<T>`,`Dep<T>`, a by-value injectable), every provider of a trait (`Vec<Arc<dyn T>>`/`HashMap<String, Arc<dyn T>>`), an optional component (`Option<Arc<T>>`), or a resolver-backed value such as`Cfg<T>`. Resolution walks the request → singleton scope chain and constructs a fresh instance when the target is a`Transient`.
- [Scope](https://docs.rs/struct.ScopeHandle.html)- Handle
- The per-request DI scope, carried in request extensions.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- Why an `Inject``500 Internal Server Error`(and log the cause).

# overseerd_axum::middleware - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/overseerd-axum/0.9.1/overseerd_axum/middleware/index.html

## Expand description

DI-backed middleware: an additive, optional path alongside plain `tower`/axum middleware.

`AxumAppBuilder::layer` takes any standard `tower::Layer` directly — `tower-http`, a
hand-written `axum::middleware::from_fn`, anything already written against axum’s own
attach points keeps working unmodified. [ AxumMiddleware](https://docs.rs/trait.AxumMiddleware.html) only adds value on top of that
for the specific case where the middleware itself wants dependency injection: a

`#[component]`
implementing it is resolved once (as a DI singleton) and shared across every attach point
(global, controller, path) it’s registered at, instead of being constructed per attach point.## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Axum](https://docs.rs/trait.AxumMiddleware.html)- Middleware
- DI-backed middleware: intercepts a request before/after axum’s handler dispatch.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [as_](https://docs.rs/fn.as_layer.html)- layer
- Adapts a resolved middleware singleton into a plain `tower::Layer`, so it composes with axum’s own`Router::layer`/`route_layer`/`MethodRouter::layer`alongside any standard tower/axum middleware registered the same way.

# overseerd_axum::request_meta - Rust

## Expand description

Native HTTP request data, seeded into every request scope.

Mirrors how the RPC protocol seeds `PeerInfo` into its connection scope: a factory-less,
by-value [ ComponentDescriptor](https://docs.rs/overseerd-di/0.9.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/overseerd_di/descriptors/component/struct.ComponentDescriptor.html) whose instance is supplied at scope-open time rather than
constructed, so a request-scoped component (or a handler, via

[) can depend on the request’s method, URI, headers, and cookies without axum’s own extractors ever entering the DI graph.](https://docs.rs/extract/struct.Inject.html)

# overseerd_axum::scope - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/overseerd-axum/0.9.1/overseerd_axum/scope/index.html

## Expand description

The axum protocol’s component scopes.

HTTP is request-oriented: axum does not surface a connection lifecycle to plain HTTP
handlers, so an HTTP request opens a single [ Request](https://docs.rs/struct.Request.html) scope parented directly at the

[root. A](https://docs.rs/overseerd-core/0.9.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/overseerd_core/scope/struct.Singleton.html)

`Singleton`**WebSocket**connection, by contrast, is long-lived and multiplexes many messages, so it opens a

[scope once per upgraded socket and a fresh](https://docs.rs/struct.Connection.html)

`Connection`[scope per inbound message parented at it — mirroring the RPC connection/request chain.](https://docs.rs/struct.Request.html)

`Request``Connection` therefore only matters for WebSocket controllers; a plain
HTTP app never opens it. Both slot between the universal `Singleton` (root) and
[anchors.](https://docs.rs/overseerd-core/0.9.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/overseerd_core/scope/struct.Transient.html)

`Transient`## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Connection](https://docs.rs/struct.Connection.html)
- A per-connection scope: one live WebSocket connection. Outlives the messages multiplexed over
it, so it ranks above `Request``Request`
- [Request](https://docs.rs/struct.Request.html)
- A per-request scope: one inbound HTTP request, or one inbound WebSocket message.

---

# overseerd_axum::stream - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/overseerd-axum/0.9.1/overseerd_axum/stream/index.html

## Expand description

Streamed response bodies — the streaming analogue of the unary body wrappers
(`Json<T>`/`Form<T>`).

The wrapper *type* is the framing, never a separate format parameter: a handler returns
[ Ndjson<S>](https://docs.rs/struct.Ndjson.html) (newline-delimited JSON over the item stream

`S`) or [(raw](https://docs.rs/struct.RawStream.html)

`RawStream<S>``Bytes` chunks), and that one type picks both the encoding and the `Content-Type`. A new
framing — multipart, length-delimited, … — is just another wrapper that is an
[; nothing is locked to one format.](https://docs.rs/axum-core/0.5.6/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/axum_core/response/into_response/trait.IntoResponse.html)

`IntoResponse`Because handlers are ordinary axum handlers, the server side needs no macro or capability
support: returning a wrapper *is* the response. (A bare `impl Stream` cannot be returned
directly — Rust’s orphan rule blocks an `IntoResponse` impl for it — so the newtype is the
thinnest possible wrapper, and `Ndjson(stream)` reads no heavier than the stream itself.)

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Ndjson](https://docs.rs/struct.Ndjson.html)
- A newline-delimited-JSON streamed response (`application/x-ndjson`): each item of the wrapped stream is serialized to one JSON line.
- [RawStream](https://docs.rs/struct.RawStream.html)
- A raw byte-stream response (`application/octet-stream`): each`Bytes`
- [Stream](https://docs.rs/struct.StreamBody.html)- Body
- A streamed **request body**, deframed into items for a`#[stream]`handler parameter. The server reads the request body through axum’s streaming and yields`T`per NDJSON line (a transport/decode error ends the stream, logged). A handler writes`#[stream] items: impl Stream<Item = T>`; the macro extracts via this and hands the handler the inner stream.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Stream](https://docs.rs/trait.StreamEncode.html)- Encode
- Frames a stream of items into the bytes of a streamed body — the encode dual of
[`ndjson_decode`], used by the client to send a`#[stream]`request body. The framing wrapper (`Ndjson`/`RawStream`/a custom one) picks the wire format; pluggable, never hard-wired.

---

# AppRegistry in overseerd_axum - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/overseerd-axum/0.9.1/overseerd_axum/struct.AppRegistry.html

```
pub struct AppRegistry {
    pub components:
```
[Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html)<[ComponentDescriptor](https://docs.rs/overseerd-di/0.9.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/overseerd_di/descriptors/component/struct.ComponentDescriptor.html)>,
    pub providers: [Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html)<[ProviderDescriptor](https://docs.rs/overseerd-di/0.9.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/overseerd_di/descriptors/component/struct.ProviderDescriptor.html)>,
    pub config_bindings: [Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html)<[ConfigBinding](https://docs.rs/overseerd-config/0.9.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/overseerd_config/managed/struct.ConfigBinding.html)>,
}## Expand description

Holds the *agnostic* component, provider, and config-binding descriptors of an app —
declarations only. Runtime instances live in the
[ ScopeContainer](https://docs.rs/overseerd-di/0.9.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/overseerd_di/container/struct.ScopeContainer.html).

Wraps the DI engine’s [ ComponentRegistry](https://docs.rs/overseerd-di/0.9.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/overseerd_di/registry/struct.ComponentRegistry.html) (component/provider graph) with the config
bindings, and runs the cross-cutting validation the component graph alone cannot
(config edges). Protocol-specific declarations (services/routes) live in the protocol
plugin, not here, so this stays usable by any protocol.

## Fields[§](https://docs.rs#fields)

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.components)

`components: `[Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html)<[ComponentDescriptor](https://docs.rs/overseerd-di/0.9.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/overseerd_di/descriptors/component/struct.ComponentDescriptor.html)>[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.providers)

`providers: `[Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html)<[ProviderDescriptor](https://docs.rs/overseerd-di/0.9.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/overseerd_di/descriptors/component/struct.ProviderDescriptor.html)>[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.config_bindings)

`config_bindings: `[Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html)<[ConfigBinding](https://docs.rs/overseerd-config/0.9.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/overseerd_config/managed/struct.ConfigBinding.html)>Config bindings (a config type bound to a property path). Populated from the auto-discovered config bindings slice and from explicit builder bindings.

# AppRuntime in overseerd_axum - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/overseerd-axum/0.9.1/overseerd_axum/struct.AppRuntime.html

`pub struct AppRuntime { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

Everything a protocol needs to drive requests through DI, cheaply cloneable.

Agnostic to any particular protocol: it holds the built root scope, the per-scope
construction orders keyed by scope name (computed from the protocol’s declared
scope chain), the resolved component set, and the hook manager. A protocol opens
its scopes through [ open_scope](https://docs.rs/struct.AppRuntime.html#method.open_scope), naming each scope from its own
chain.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

#### pub async fn [open_scope](https://docs.rs#method.open_scope)(
    &self,
    scope: &'static dyn [Scope](https://docs.rs/overseerd-core/0.9.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/overseerd_core/scope/trait.Scope.html),
    parent: [Arc](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/sync/struct.Arc.html)<[ScopeContainer](https://docs.rs/overseerd-di/0.9.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/overseerd_di/container/struct.ScopeContainer.html)>,

Opens a child container for `scope` over `parent`, seeding `seeds` and
constructing that scope’s precomputed order (empty when the scope holds nothing
constructable). An empty, unseeded scope is skipped — `parent` is returned
unchanged. `scope` must be one the app was built for (in the protocol’s chain).

The cloneable handle this component is stored in the container as, and
injected by.

`Arc<Self>` by default (auto-wrapped); a type that manages
its own sharing — typically because it is internally `Arc` and cheap to
clone — may set this to `Self` via `#[component(by_value)]`, so it is

# Plugin in overseerd_axum - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/overseerd-axum/0.9.1/overseerd_axum/trait.Plugin.html

`pub trait Plugin: `[Default](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/default/trait.Default.html) {
    // Required method
    fn [register](https://docs.rs#tymethod.register)(&self, registry: &mut [AppRegistry](https://docs.rs/struct.AppRegistry.html));
    // Provided method
    fn [auto_discover](https://docs.rs#method.auto_discover)(&mut self) { ... }
}## Expand description

A general extension unit applied to an app while it is built.

A plugin is the builder-time accumulator for an extension: it starts empty
([ Default](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/default/trait.Default.html)), gathers protocol-specific configuration through the builder, folds its
link-time-discovered variants in on

`auto_discover`, and contributes DI descriptors
into the registry before the container is built. A plugin need not serve traffic —
that is the job of the [sub-trait. Background behavior rides the components a plugin registers (via their own](https://docs.rs/trait.ProtocolPlugin.html)

`ProtocolPlugin``#[hook]`s).## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

## Provided Methods[§](https://docs.rs#provided-methods)

[Source](https://docs.rs/overseerd-app/0.9.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/overseerd_app/protocol.rs.html#26)#### fn [auto_discover](https://docs.rs#method.auto_discover)(&mut self)

[Source](https://docs.rs/overseerd-app/0.9.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/src/overseerd_app/protocol.rs.html#26)

#### fn [auto_discover](https://docs.rs#method.auto_discover)(&mut self)

Folds this plugin’s link-time-registered component variants (e.g. the RPC
`SERVICES` slice) into the accumulator. Called from `AppBuilder::auto_discover`.
Default: nothing to discover.

## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait is **not** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

---

# Serve in overseerd_axum - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/overseerd-axum/0.9.1/overseerd_axum/trait.Serve.html

`pub trait Serve<E>: `[Protocol](https://docs.rs/trait.Protocol.html) {
    // Required method
    fn [serve](https://docs.rs#tymethod.serve)(
        self,
        runtime: [AppRuntime](https://docs.rs/struct.AppRuntime.html),
        shutdown: [ShutdownSignal](https://docs.rs/struct.ShutdownSignal.html),
        endpoint: E,
    ) -> impl [Future](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/future/future/trait.Future.html)<Output = [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.unit.html), Self::[Error](https://docs.rs/trait.Protocol.html#associatedtype.Error)>> + [Send](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Send.html);
}## Expand description

Serves a built protocol over a concrete endpoint type `E`. Kept separate from
[ Protocol](https://docs.rs/trait.Protocol.html) so one protocol can serve many endpoint types — RPC over any transport, a
future HTTP protocol over a

`SocketAddr`. The serve loop only needs to watch `endpoint`
and `shutdown`; lifecycle and reload are handled by the caller (`App::serve`).## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

    self,
    runtime: [AppRuntime](https://docs.rs/struct.AppRuntime.html),
    shutdown: [ShutdownSignal](https://docs.rs/struct.ShutdownSignal.html),
    endpoint: E,
) -> impl [Future](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/future/future/trait.Future.html)<Output = [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.unit.html), Self::[Error](https://docs.rs/trait.Protocol.html#associatedtype.Error)>> + [Send](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Send.html)

## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/overseerd_app/app.rs.html#490-492)#### pub fn [hook_manager](https://docs.rs#method.hook_manager)(&self) -> [HookManager](https://docs.rs/overseerd-hooks/0.9.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/overseerd_hooks/struct.HookManager.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/overseerd_app/app.rs.html#490-492)

#### pub fn [hook_manager](https://docs.rs#method.hook_manager)(&self) -> [HookManager](https://docs.rs/overseerd-hooks/0.9.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/overseerd_hooks/struct.HookManager.html)

The hook manager, for running lifecycle/event hooks by kind.

Serves the app’s protocol over `endpoint` until ctrl-c or a shutdown signal.

The agnostic envelope: runs startup hooks, spawns config-reload triggers, bridges
ctrl-c to the shutdown signal, then hands the runtime + shutdown signal to the
protocol’s [ Serve](https://docs.rs/protocol/trait.Serve.html) impl. Shutdown hooks run on the way out.

Generic over the [ ProtocolPlugin](https://docs.rs/protocol/trait.ProtocolPlugin.html) it installs. The agnostic builder methods (config,

# controller in overseerd_axum - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/overseerd-axum/0.9.1/overseerd_axum/attr.controller.html

`#[controller]`## Expand description

The axum controller macros (`#[controller]`, `#[handlers]`, the route attributes), owned by
this protocol crate. Their generated code roots plugin types at this crate
(`::overseerd_axum::*`) by default, or at `::overseerd::axum::*` under the `facade` feature —
so they work whether `overseerd-axum` is used directly or through the `overseerd` facade. The
core macros (`app!`, `#[component]`, …) come from `overseerd` (the always-present core).
Declares a **controller** — a router component exposing HTTP routes.

`#[controller]` is `ComponentArgs<AxumRouter>`: a `#[component]` (field-injected singleton)
plus the controller surface — a [ Controller](https://docs.rs/overseerd_axum/trait.Controller.html) impl,
the controller’s

`{Controller}Routes` slice, and its `ControllerDescriptor`. Routes are
added by `#[handlers]` impls. Accepts the component keys plus `path` (the base path) and
`routes_slice`.
